nameStory: The name 'pumpkin' comes from the Greek word 'pepon,' meaning 'large melon,' which the French adapted to 'pompon' and the English eventually transformed into 'pumpkin.' American colonists borrowed this term from European settlers who were amazed by these huge, orange native fruits that Indigenous peoples had been cultivating for thousands of years.
description: American pumpkin is a sprawling vine that produces the classic orange jack-o'-lantern pumpkins we all know and love. The plant sends out long, thick stems that can stretch 10-20 feet across the ground, with large, lobed leaves that feel rough and scratchy to the touch. During summer, it produces bright yellow-orange flowers that are surprisingly large - about 4 inches across - followed by the familiar round, ribbed fruits that can range from softball-sized to massive 100+ pound giants.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, heart-shaped leaves with 3-5 pointed lobes and rough, sandpapery texture that feels scratchy against your skin

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow-orange trumpet-shaped flowers about 4 inches across with five petals that feel soft and velvety; male flowers appear first on long stems, female flowers have tiny fruits at their base

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Round to oblong orange fruits with deep vertical ridges and a hard, smooth shell; stem end has a distinctive thick, corky 'handle'

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Long trailing vines that sprawl across the ground with thick, hollow stems covered in prickly hairs that feel rough to touch

idTips.label: Tendrils
idTips.description: Curly, spiraling tendrils that reach out from the vine to grab onto supports, feeling springy and flexible when fresh

habitat: In New England, you'll find pumpkins growing in cultivated fields, gardens, and farmyards, typically in rich, well-drained soil with full sun exposure. They occasionally escape cultivation and can be found growing wild in disturbed areas, field edges, and compost piles. These heat-loving plants thrive in the warmer, southern parts of New England but can grow throughout the region with proper care.

seasonality.spring: Seeds are planted after the last frost, usually late May in New England. Young seedlings emerge with two large, oval seed leaves followed by the first true lobed leaves.
seasonality.summer: Vines spread rapidly and bright yellow flowers bloom from July through August. Male flowers appear first, followed by female flowers that will develop into fruit.
seasonality.fall: Pumpkins ripen to their classic orange color from September through October. The vines begin to die back after the first frost, but mature fruits can withstand light frosts.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts are killed by hard frost. Only harvested pumpkins remain, stored indoors or slowly decomposing in fields.

funFact: Pumpkins are technically berries! In botanical terms, they're a special type of berry called a 'pepo' (yes, the same root as the species name), which means they have a hard rind and fleshy interior with seeds embedded in the flesh - just like watermelons and cucumbers.
confusionNotes: Wild pumpkins can be confused with other squash varieties, but true American pumpkins have distinctively corky, ridged stems and tend to be more perfectly round. Summer squashes like zucchini have similar flowers and leaves but produce elongated fruits that are harvested when small and tender.
contextualKnowledge: What we call 'pumpkins' actually includes several different species and varieties - jack-o'-lantern pumpkins, pie pumpkins, and many decorative gourds can all be the same species (Cucurbita pepo) but different cultivated varieties. This is why pumpkins can look so different from each other while being essentially the same plant.
compareHints: American pumpkin differs from winter squash (Cucurbita maxima) by having distinctly ridged, corky stems rather than soft, rounded ones, and more angular leaf lobes. Unlike Cucurbita moschata varieties, American pumpkin leaves are more deeply lobed and feel rougher to the touch, plus the fruits tend to be more perfectly round rather than elongated.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to American pumpkin (Cucurbita pepo), winter squash tends to have rounder, less-ridged fruits with thicker flesh and often more varied colors and shapes.
